claim: TANGO1 assembles into a ring around ER exit sites (ERES).
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident protein TANGO1 assembles into a ring around ER exit sites (ERES), and links procollagens in the ER lumen to COPII machinery, tethers, and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) in the cytoplasm (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018.

claim: TANGO1 links procollagens in the ER lumen to COPII machinery, tethers, and ERGIC in the cytoplasm.
source: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER)-resident protein TANGO1 assembles into a ring around ER exit sites (ERES), and links procollagens in the ER lumen to COPII machinery, tethers, and ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) in the cytoplasm (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018.

claim: A TANGO1 ring, by acting as a linactant, stabilizes the open neck of a nascent COPII bud.
source: Our results indicate that a TANGO1 ring, by acting as a linactant, stabilizes the open neck of a nascent COPII bud.
evidence: The claim is based on the theoretical modeling results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Elongation of a COPII bud into a transport intermediate commensurate with bulky procollagens is facilitated by relieving membrane tension, possibly by TANGO1-mediated fusion of retrograde ERGIC membranes.
source: Elongation of such a bud into a transport intermediate commensurate with bulky procollagens is then facilitated by two complementary mechanisms: (i) by relieving membrane tension, possibly by TANGO1-mediated fusion of retrograde ERGIC membranes and (ii) by force application.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results and speculative reasoning about ERGIC membrane fusion.

claim: Elongation of a COPII bud into a transport intermediate commensurate with bulky procollagens is facilitated by force application.
source: Elongation of such a bud into a transport intermediate commensurate with bulky procollagens is then facilitated by two complementary mechanisms: (i) by relieving membrane tension, possibly by TANGO1-mediated fusion of retrograde ERGIC membranes and (ii) by force application.
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical modeling results and speculative reasoning about force generation.

claim: Collagens form the extracellular matrix (ECM).
source: Multicellularity requires not only the secretion of signaling proteins –such as neurotransmitters, cytokines, and hormones– to regulate cell-to-cell communication, but also of biomechanical matrices composed primarily of proteins such as collagens, which form the extracellular matrix (ECM) (Kadler et al., 2007; Mouw et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kadler et al., 2007 and Mouw et al., 2014.

claim: Extracellular assemblies of collagens are necessary for tissue biogenesis and maintenance.
source: These extracellular assemblies of collagens are necessary for tissue biogenesis and maintenance.
evidence: The claim is based on established scientific knowledge about collagen function.

claim: Procollagens fold and trimerize into a characteristic triple-helical, rigid structure.
source: After their glycosylation, procollagens fold and trimerize into a characteristic triple-helical, rigid structure, which, depending on the isoform, may extend several hundred nm in length (McCaughey and Stephens, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughey and Stephens, 2019.

claim: Procollagen triple-helical structures may extend several hundred nm in length depending on the isoform.
source: After their glycosylation, procollagens fold and trimerize into a characteristic triple-helical, rigid structure, which, depending on the isoform, may extend several hundred nm in length (McCaughey and Stephens, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughey and Stephens, 2019.

claim: Bulky procollagens are exported from the ER at specialized export domains termed ER exit sites (ERES) in a COPII-dependent manner.
source: These bulky procollagens are then exported from the ER at specialized export domains, termed ER exit sites (ERES), in a COPII-dependent manner.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about procollagen export.

claim: Polymerized coats such as COPI, COPII, and clathrin coats usually adopt spherical shapes.
source: Polymerized coats, such as COPI, COPII, and clathrin coats, usually adopt spherical shapes –which bend the membrane underneath to form small vesicles of ~60–90 nm in diameter (Faini et al., 2013), although helical arrangements of COPII coats have been observed (Zanetti et al., 2013; Ma and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Faini et al., 2013, Zanetti et al., 2013, and Ma and Goldberg, 2016.

claim: Polymerized coats bend the membrane underneath to form small vesicles of ~60–90 nm in diameter.
source: Polymerized coats, such as COPI, COPII, and clathrin coats, usually adopt spherical shapes –which bend the membrane underneath to form small vesicles of ~60–90 nm in diameter (Faini et al., 2013), although helical arrangements of COPII coats have been observed (Zanetti et al., 2013; Ma and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Faini et al., 2013.

claim: Helical arrangements of COPII coats have been observed.
source: Polymerized coats, such as COPI, COPII, and clathrin coats, usually adopt spherical shapes –which bend the membrane underneath to form small vesicles of ~60–90 nm in diameter (Faini et al., 2013), although helical arrangements of COPII coats have been observed (Zanetti et al., 2013; Ma and Goldberg, 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zanetti et al., 2013 and Ma and Goldberg, 2016.

claim: Membrane bending by coats is promoted when the energy gain of coat polymerization is larger than the elastic energy of membrane deformation.
source: Membrane bending by coats is promoted when the energy gain of coat polymerization is larger than the elastic energy of membrane deformation (Derganc et al., 2013; Scheve et al., 2013; Kozlov et al., 2014; Saleem et al., 2015; Day and Stachowiak, 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to multiple studies on membrane mechanics.

claim: The SH3-like domain of TANGO1 binds procollagen via HSP47 in the lumen of the ER.
source: In the lumen of the ER, the SH3-like domain of TANGO1 binds procollagen via HSP47 (Saito et al., 2009; Ishikawa et al., 2016; Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009 and Ishikawa et al., 2016, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The PRD of TANGO1 interacts with the COPII components Sec23A and Sec16.
source: The PRD of TANGO1 interacts with the COPII components Sec23A and Sec16 (Saito et al., 2009; Ma and Goldberg, 2016; Maeda et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2009, Ma and Goldberg, 2016, and Maeda et al., 2017.

claim: The CC1 domain of TANGO1 binds the NBAS/RINT1/ZW10 (NRZ) tethering complex to recruit ERGIC membranes.
source: the CC1 domain binds the NBAS/RINT1/ZW10 (NRZ) tethering complex to recruit ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) membranes and also drives self-association amongst TANGO1 proteins (Santos et al., 2015; Raote et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Santos et al., 2015 and Raote et al., 2018.

claim: The CC1 domain of TANGO1 drives self-association amongst TANGO1 proteins.
source: the CC1 domain binds the NBAS/RINT1/ZW10 (NRZ) tethering complex to recruit ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) membranes and also drives self-association amongst TANGO1 proteins (Santos et al., 2015; Raote et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Santos et al., 2015 and Raote et al., 2018.

claim: The CC2 domain of TANGO1 oligomerizes with proteins of the TANGO1 family such as cTAGE5.
source: and the CC2 domain oligomerizes with proteins of the TANGO1 family (such as cTAGE5) (Saito et al., 2011; Maeda et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Saito et al., 2011 and Maeda et al., 2016.

claim: A disease-causing mutation in TANGO1 in a human family results in a substantial fraction of TANGO1 protein being truncated and lacking its cytosolic functions, leading to collagen export defects.
source: For instance, a recent report identified a disease-causing mutation in TANGO1 in a human family, which results in a substantial fraction of TANGO1 protein being truncated and lacking its cytosolic functions, leading to collagen export defects (Lekszas et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Lekszas et al., 2020.

claim: TANGO1 organizes at the ERES into ring-like structures of ~200 nm in lumenal diameter that corral COPII components.
source: These studies revealed that TANGO1 organizes at the ERES into ring-like structures, of ~200 nm in lumenal diameter, that corral COPII components.
evidence: The claim is based on STED nanoscopy studies referenced in the manuscript.

claim: TANGO1 rings are present in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: Moreover, two independent studies showed that TANGO1 rings are also present in Drosophila melanogaster (Liu et al., 2017; Reynolds et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017 and Reynolds et al., 2019.

claim: TANGO1 rings are organized by lateral self-interactions amongst TANGO1-like proteins.
source: we combined STED nanoscopy with genetic manipulations and established that TANGO1 rings are organized by (i) lateral self-interactions amongst TANGO1-like proteins, (ii) radial interactions with COPII subunits, and (iii) tethering of small ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) vesicles to assist in the formation of a procollagen-containing export intermediate (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018 and experimental data from STED nanoscopy.

claim: TANGO1 rings are organized by radial interactions with COPII subunits.
source: we combined STED nanoscopy with genetic manipulations and established that TANGO1 rings are organized by (i) lateral self-interactions amongst TANGO1-like proteins, (ii) radial interactions with COPII subunits, and (iii) tethering of small ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) vesicles to assist in the formation of a procollagen-containing export intermediate (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018 and experimental data from STED nanoscopy.

claim: TANGO1 rings are organized by tethering of small ERGIC vesicles to assist in the formation of a procollagen-containing export intermediate.
source: we combined STED nanoscopy with genetic manipulations and established that TANGO1 rings are organized by (i) lateral self-interactions amongst TANGO1-like proteins, (ii) radial interactions with COPII subunits, and (iii) tethering of small ER-Golgi intermediate compartment (ERGIC) vesicles to assist in the formation of a procollagen-containing export intermediate (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018 and experimental data from STED nanoscopy.

claim: TANGO1 family of proteins can be effectively described as a single species for modeling purposes.
source: Given the complexity of the system and the lack of quantitative biochemical data regarding the interactions amongst the different TANGO1 and COPII components, we assume for our modeling purposes that the TANGO1 family of proteins (TANGO1, cTAGE5 and TANGO1-Short) can be effectively described as a single species, to which we will simply refer as TANGO1.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption stated explicitly in the manuscript.

claim: COPII subunits polymerize on the ER membrane forming a coat of specific curvature.
source: Hypothesis 2: COPII subunits polymerize on the ER membrane forming a coat of specific curvature.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental hypothesis of the model, based on established knowledge.

claim: COPII coat assembly typically results in spherical carriers of 60–90 nm.
source: Polymerization of COPII subunits into spherical lattices induces curvature on the underlying membrane, typically resulting in spherical carriers of 60–90 nm (Faini et al., 2013; Aridor, 2018; Peotter et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Faini et al., 2013, Aridor, 2018, and Peotter et al., 2019.

claim: TANGO1 molecules have a propensity to assemble into rings as a result of protein-protein interactions between TANGO1-family proteins.
source: Hypothesis 3: TANGO1 molecules have a propensity to assemble into rings as a result of protein-protein interactions between TANGO1-family proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental hypothesis of the model, supported by multiple experimental observations.

claim: There is a direct 1:1 binding between TANGO1 and cTAGE5 CC2 domains.
source: This hypothesis is based on the observations that: (i) TANGO1 is seen in ring-like filamentous assemblies of specific size by STED nanoscopy (Raote et al., 2017; Roux, 2018); (ii) there is a direct 1:1 binding between TANGO1 and cTAGE5 CC2 domains (Saito et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Saito et al., 2011.

claim: TANGO1-Short and cTAGE5 can form oligomers and oligomeric complexes together with Sec12 and TANGO1.
source: (iii) TANGO1-Short and cTAGE5 can form oligomers and oligomeric complexes together with Sec12 and TANGO1 (Maeda et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Maeda et al., 2016.

claim: TANGO1 and TANGO1-Short can directly homo-dimerize by their CC1 domains.
source: (iv) TANGO1 and TANGO1-Short can directly homo-dimerize by their CC1 domains (Raote et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018.

claim: TANGO1 has a binding affinity to the peripheral COPII coat subunits, helping stabilize the COPII domain boundary by effectively reducing its line energy.
source: Hypothesis 4: TANGO1 has a binding affinity to the peripheral COPII coat subunits, helping stabilize the COPII domain boundary by effectively reducing its line energy.
evidence: This is stated as a fundamental hypothesis of the model, supported by experimental observations.

claim: TANGO1 acts as a linactant by filling unsatisfied binding sites of the COPII coat edges and therefore effectively lowering its line tension.
source: In physical terms, this hypothesis is equivalent to state that TANGO1 acts as a linactant by filling unsatisfied binding sites of the COPII coat edges and therefore effectively lowering its line tension (Figure 1B; Trabelsi et al., 2008, Saleem et al., 2015; Glick, 2017).
evidence: The claim is based on physical interpretation of the model, supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: Functional TANGO1 drastically modifies the dynamics and outcome of bud formation compared to inert TANGO1.
source: In contrast, functional TANGO1 drastically modifies the dynamics and outcome of bud formation (see Figure 2B and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Functional TANGO1 shortens the nucleation stage of COPII coat formation.
source: First, the nucleation stage is shortened, suggesting that TANGO1 can facilitate the nucleation of the COPII coat in the presence of a small force perturbation at the membrane.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: Functional TANGO1 stabilizes COPII buds into shallow, incomplete transport intermediates with shape parameter around η≃0.8.
source: Second, instead of growing to the point where the neck closes, we find that the shape parameter reaches a maximum around η≃0.9, before slightly decreasing to a stable height around η≃0.8.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results.

claim: TANGO1 self-assembles into a high-density ring-like structure around the COPII coat that stabilizes the bud into a shallow, incomplete transport intermediate.
source: As seen from the corresponding snapshots (Figure 2B(i–iii)), this dynamic evolution is accompanied by the self-assembly of a high-density TANGO1 ring-like structure around the COPII coat that stabilizes the bud into a shallow, incomplete transport intermediate.
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Simulation results of TANGO1 rings encircling COPII components are in agreement with experimental observations of TANGO1 rings in procollagen-rich membrane patches.
source: These simulation results are in agreement with experimental observations of TANGO1 rings encircling COPII components in procollagen-rich membrane patches (Raote et al., 2017; Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim compares modeling results with experimental data from cited studies.

claim: ERGIC53-containing vesicles are recruited to the ERES by TANGO1 via tethering complexes.
source: Such scenario is motivated by our previous experimental data showing that (i) ERGIC53-containing vesicles are recruited to the ERES by TANGO1 via tethering complexes (Nogueira et al., 2014; Santos et al., 2015; Raote et al., 2018), presumably enabling their fusion to the ER membrane
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Nogueira et al., 2014, Santos et al., 2015, and Raote et al., 2018.

claim: Cells depleted of the tethering factors recruited by TANGO1 to ERES showed a reduction of ~70–80% in collagen secretion.
source: and (ii) cells depleted of the tethering factors recruited by TANGO1 to ERES showed a reduction of ~70–80% in collagen secretion (Raote et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2018 and experimental data.

claim: The '2-pearl' shape of the transport intermediate corresponds to a height of about 300 nm, a typical length of trimerized procollagen I molecules.
source: Interestingly, the '2-pearl' shape corresponds to a height of about 300 nm, a typical length of trimerized procollagen I molecules (McCaughey and Stephens, 2019).
evidence: The claim compares modeling results with known procollagen dimensions from McCaughey and Stephens, 2019.

claim: TANGO1 self-organizes around COPII coats and stabilizes shallow buds at physiological membrane tensions.
source: Altogether, our computational results support the scenario by which TANGO1 self-organizes around COPII coats and stabilizes shallow buds at physiological membrane tensions.
evidence: The claim summarizes the computational modeling results.

claim: The stability of shallow buds might facilitate procollagen recruitment and packaging by TANGO1 as well as the recruitment of ERGIC membranes to the ERES.
source: The stability of shallow buds might facilitate procollagen recruitment and packaging by TANGO1 as well as the recruitment of ERGIC membranes to the ERES.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from modeling results.

claim: Procollagen located at the neck of the growing carrier acts as a means to sterically prevent carrier scission.
source: We suggest that procollagen located at the neck of the growing carrier acts as a means to sterically prevent carrier scission.
evidence: The claim is a speculative suggestion based on modeling considerations.

claim: At low membrane tension, the growth of the metastable bud can be triggered by a small perturbation such as thermal fluctuations or a mechanical perturbation in the system.
source: At low membrane tension, the growth of the metastable bud can be triggered by a small perturbation – such as thermal fluctuations or a mechanical perturbation in the system – and might be facilitated by transient uncapping (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The tension-mediated growth of large transport intermediates is effectively a ratchet-like mechanism.
source: Overall, the tension-mediated growth of large transport intermediates is effectively a ratchet-like mechanism, where the difference between the energy barriers guarantees an almost unidirectional evolution of the system leading to the transport intermediate growth.
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results and physical interpretation.

claim: TANGO1 expands the parameter space at which stable shallow buds are obtained.
source: Interestingly, the presence of functional TANGO1 dramatically widens the parameter space at which stable shallow buds are obtained.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of computational modeling results with and without functional TANGO1.

claim: The capping-uncapping transition of COPII coat by TANGO1 plays an important role in determining the transition between equilibrium-budded states.
source: As seen in Figures 4 and 5, the capping-uncapping transition of COPII coat by TANGO1 plays an important role in determining the transition between equilibrium-budded states.
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Capping of COPII components by TANGO1 is promoted by large values of the TANGO1-COPII interaction and prevented by large TANGO1 filament bending rigidities.
source: These analytical results highlight how capping of COPII components by TANGO1 is promoted by large values of the TANGO1-COPII interaction, Δλ, and prevented by large TANGO1 filament bending rigidities, κT (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: TANGO1 capping significantly expands the regions where stable shallow buds are energetically favored.
source: Remarkably, we find once again that TANGO1 capping significantly expands the regions where stable shallow buds are energetically favored.
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results from shape diagrams.

claim: The presence of a TANGO1 ring capping COPII subunits induced the formation of shapes with larger neck radii.
source: In addition, the presence of a TANGO1 ring capping COPII subunits induced the formation of shapes with larger neck radii (Figure 6B,C, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results shown in Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Having a point force shifts the capping-uncapping and transport intermediate growth transitions toward lower COPII binding energies and higher membrane tensions.
source: As shown in Figure 7A,B, we found that having a point force shifts the capping-uncapping and transport intermediate growth transitions toward lower COPII binding energies and higher membrane tensions.
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The critical force of 1.4 pN is in the same order of magnitude of the force generated by molecular actin polymerization.
source: which, for comparison, is in the same order of magnitude of the force generated by molecular actin polymerization (Footer et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim compares the calculated force with known forces from Footer et al., 2007.

claim: The critical force of 1.4 pN is an order of magnitude smaller than typical force required to extract a membrane tethers.
source: and an order of magnitude smaller than typical force required to extract a membrane tethers (Derényi et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim compares the calculated force with known forces from Derényi et al., 2002.

claim: The formation of large transport intermediates can be greatly facilitated in the presence of TANGO1 by forces of physiological ranges oriented toward the cytosol.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the formation of large transport intermediates can be greatly facilitated in the presence of TANGO1 by forces of physiological ranges oriented toward the cytosol.
evidence: The claim is based on analytical modeling results.

claim: The shape of the elongated carrier is a pearled tubule according to the dynamic model.
source: Finally, the results of our dynamic model show that the shape of the elongated carrier is a pearled tubule (Figure 3D and Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: The claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The fission of the upstream pearls is prevented by a steric hindrance of the procollagen molecules packed inside the tubule.
source: The fission of the upstream pearls is prevented in our model by a steric hindrance of the procollagen molecules packed inside the tubule (Figure 8E).
evidence: The claim is based on modeling assumptions illustrated in Figure 8E.

claim: TANGO1 is indirectly required to prevent the fission of upstream necks because it is the receptor molecule that binds procollagen and packs it to facilitate its export.
source: Since TANGO1 is the receptor molecule that binds procollagen and packs it to facilitate its export (Saito et al., 2009), TANGO1 is indirectly required to prevent the fission of upstream necks.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the model and citation to Saito et al., 2009.

claim: The large transport intermediate is converted into a tunnel connecting ER to the ERGIC/early Golgi cisternae.
source: We previously proposed that the large transport intermediate is converted into a tunnel connecting ER to the ERGIC/early Golgi cisternae (Raote and Malhotra, 2019).
evidence: The claim is based on a previous proposal cited as Raote and Malhotra, 2019.

claim: The role of a TANGO1 ring would be to prevent lipid mixing between transiently connected organelles by acting as a diffusion barrier.
source: If so, an appealing possibility is that, at this stage, the role of a TANGO1 ring would be to prevent lipid mixing between these transiently connected organelles by acting as a diffusion barrier (Raote et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is a speculative possibility supported by citation to Raote et al., 2020.

claim: Changes in membrane tension have been described to affect rates of exocytosis and endocytosis at the plasma membrane.
source: Changes in membrane tension have been described to affect rates of exocytosis and endocytosis at the plasma membrane (Apodaca, 2002; Kosmalska et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Apodaca, 2002, Kosmalska et al., 2015, and Wu et al., 2017.

claim: A theoretical model has established a crucial role for membrane tension in modulating the budding of clathrin-coated vesicles.
source: Interestingly, a theoretical model has also established a crucial role for membrane tension in modulating the budding of clathrin-coated vesicles (Hassinger et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Hassinger et al., 2017.

claim: Atlastin-mediated maintenance of ER membrane tension is required for the efficient mobility of cargo proteins.
source: Furthermore, it has been recently proposed that Atlastin-mediated maintenance of ER membrane tension is required for the efficient mobility of cargo proteins (Niu et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Niu et al., 2019.

claim: The formation of intra-lumenal vesicles in endosomes is regulated by membrane tension.
source: and that the formation of intra-lumenal vesicles in endosomes is also regulated by membrane tension (Mercier et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Mercier et al., 2020.

claim: Inter-organelle hubs such as a TANGO1-scaffolded ERES-ERGIC control the local tension homeostasis at specific membrane sub-domains and regulate the membrane flux between these organelles.
source: We suggest that inter-organelle hubs, such as a TANGO1-scaffolded ERES-ERGIC, control the local tension homeostasis at specific membrane sub-domains and regulate the membrane flux between these organelles.
evidence: The claim is a suggestion based on the modeling results and discussion.

claim: Procollagen export from the ER does not require the presence of an intact microtubule network.
source: It has been shown that procollagen export from the ER does not require the presence of an intact microtubule network (McCaughey et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughey et al., 2019.

claim: The ER-specific SNARE protein Syntaxin18 and the SNARE regulator SLY1 are required for procollagen export in a TANGO1-dependent manner.
source: In particular, the ER-specific SNARE protein Syntaxin18 and the SNARE regulator SLY1, both of which are involved in membrane fusion reactions at the ER, are also required for procollagen export in a TANGO1-dependent manner (Nogueira et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2014.

claim: Fusion of ERGIC membranes to the sites of procollagen export would lead to a local and transient reduction of the membrane tension.
source: Fusion of ERGIC membranes to the sites of procollagen export would lead to a local and transient reduction of the membrane tension (Sens and Turner, 2006).
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal supported by citation to Sens and Turner, 2006.

claim: TANGO1 would act as a regulator of membrane tension homeostasis to control procollagen export at the ERES.
source: In this scenario, TANGO1 would act as a regulator of membrane tension homeostasis to control procollagen export at the ERES (Figure 8C,E).
evidence: The claim is a speculative scenario proposed based on the modeling results.

claim: ERGIC membranes fuse directly or adjacently to the growing transport intermediate to allow for membrane addition and tension release.
source: We have recently proposed that ERGIC membranes fuse directly or adjacently to the growing transport intermediate to allow for membrane addition and tension release; and showed that compartment mixing can be arrested by the TANGO1 ring serving as a diffusion barrier (Raote et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is based on a recent proposal cited as Raote et al., 2020.

claim: Compartment mixing can be arrested by the TANGO1 ring serving as a diffusion barrier.
source: We have recently proposed that ERGIC membranes fuse directly or adjacently to the growing transport intermediate to allow for membrane addition and tension release; and showed that compartment mixing can be arrested by the TANGO1 ring serving as a diffusion barrier (Raote et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2020.

claim: Mechanical equilibration of the membrane shape can be theoretically estimated to be of the order of milliseconds.
source: First, mechanical equilibration of the membrane shape (τmech) can be theoretically estimated to be of the order of milliseconds (see e.g. Campelo et al., 2017; Sens and Rao, 2013), which is also in accordance to our own results from model A, where shape changes are found within few milliseconds (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on theoretical estimates from cited studies and modeling results.

claim: Membrane shape equilibrates much faster than the recovery of the membrane tension.
source: Since τσ≫τmech, membrane shape equilibrates much faster than the recovery of the membrane tension.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of time scales from theoretical estimates and measurements.

claim: TANGO1 can induce a diffusion barrier at the base of the growing bud.
source: Moreover, our recent findings that TANGO1 can induce a diffusion barrier at the base of the growing bud (Raote et al., 2020), suggest that the dynamics of tension equilibration can be even slower.
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Raote et al., 2020.

claim: HSP47 chaperone assists in folding and rigidifying procollagen.
source: Because HSP47 chaperone assists in folding (and hence in rigidifying) procollagen
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about HSP47 function.

claim: The trimerization of procollagen occurs concomitantly to its export.
source: it is tempting to speculate that the trimerization of procollagen occurs concomitantly to the its export
evidence: The claim is explicitly stated as speculation.

claim: The physical interaction between TANGO1 rings and procollagen/HSP47 could serve as a means to couple procollagen folding to force production.
source: and that the physical interaction between TANGO1 rings and procollagen/HSP47 could serve as a means to couple procollagen folding to force production.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal.

claim: TANGO1 could act as a sensor of procollagen folding to couple it with the export machinery.
source: Although the existence of this pushing force is largely speculative, it could, according to our model, promote formation of a large intermediate and hence TANGO1 could act as a sensor of procollagen folding to couple it with the export machinery.
evidence: The claim is a speculative proposal based on modeling results.

claim: Direct transport of procollagen between the ER and the Golgi complex by a short-loop pathway in the absence of large vesicles has been recently proposed.
source: By contrast, direct transport of procollagen between the ER and the Golgi complex by a short-loop pathway in the absence of large vesicles has been recently proposed (McCaughey et al., 2019)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughey et al., 2019.

claim: Fully folded procollagen required ~15 min to reach the early Golgi compartment in experiments where type I procollagen triple-helical stabilization and ER export were synchronized.
source: However, in experiments where type I procollagen triple-helical stabilization and ER export were synchronized, fully folded procollagen required ~15 min to reach the early Golgi compartment (McCaughey et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to McCaughey et al., 2019.

claim: The half-lives of COPII components on the ER membrane are of the order of a few seconds.
source: Since the half-lives of COPII components on the ER membrane are of the order of a few seconds (Forster et al., 2006)
